title: Texasweed in Rice: How to Spot It and Keep Its Seeds Out of Your Harvest
metaTitle: Texasweed in Rice Fields: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Texasweed, or salu saluyot, can mix its seeds into your rice harvest and lower grain quality. Learn to spot it early and stop it before it seeds.
excerpt: Texasweed is an upright, hairy broadleaf weed that grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Some farmers worry most about its round seeds, which can end up mixed with harvested palay. This page shows how to spot it, what it can cost you, and how to control it before it seeds.

heroImage.alt: Texasweed (Caperonia palustris), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This weed belongs to the spurge family, and its scientific name is Caperonia palustris. In some areas, farmers call it salu saluyot. The English name comes from the United States, where it troubles rice farmers too. Texasweed grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields, so it can turn up in almost any paddy. It likes wet soil and grows upright right among the rice hills.

As an annual, each plant lives for one season and then dies. It spreads only by seed. Its fruits have three parts, and each part holds one round seed. The seeds start grayish and turn dark brown as they ripen. When plants still stand at harvest, those seeds can go into the thresher along with the palay.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Texasweed
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look for an upright, branched plant with hairy stems. Rub a leaf and you will feel hairs on it too. The leaves come broad and lance shaped, with saw toothed edges, and they grow one at a time along the stem. As a broadleaf weed, it has flat leaves with netted veins. Small white flowers appear first, followed by fruits with three sections. Each section holds one round seed, grayish when young and dark brown when ripe.

items: Upright, branched plants with stems that feel hairy when you run your hand along them.
Hairy, broadly lance shaped leaves with saw toothed edges, set one at a time along the stem.
Small white flowers that come before the round, three part fruits.
Fruits split into three sections, each holding one round seed.
Seeds that start grayish and turn dark brown once mature.

blocks.text:
In the Philippines, no scientific report has shown yet that Texasweed lowers rice yield. Still, some farmers say it badly hurt the quality of their harvested grain and their net income. The problem comes at harvest, when its seeds get mixed in with the palay. Dirty grain sells for less, and that is how the weed eats into your income.

Elsewhere, the picture looks worse. In the USA, studies found that 10 plants per square meter cut the yield of drill seeded rice by 24 to 31 percent. So do not wait for local yield studies before you act.

items: Pull plants before the three part fruits form. Once seeds turn dark brown, they are ready to drop or ride into the harvest.
Walk the field before harvest and remove any plants still standing, so their seeds do not go into the thresher with your palay.
Clean your seed before the next planting or buy certified seed, since seed mixed with the grain carries the weed to new fields.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Texasweed down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

items.q: What do Filipino farmers call Texasweed?
items.a: In some areas, farmers call it salu saluyot. The name links it to saluyot, the leafy vegetable, but the two plants are not the same, so do not mistake one for the other. Its scientific name is Caperonia palustris, and it belongs to the spurge family. In the field, look for hairy stems, toothed leaves, white flowers and round seeds in three part fruits.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean or certified seed, so you do not plant the weed with your palay. Then hand weed early, before the three part fruits form, and pull any late plants before harvest. If you need a herbicide, choose one made for broadleaf weeds that suits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Does it really lower my yield?
items.a: In the Philippines, no study has reported a yield loss so far. But farmers do report lower grain quality and income when its seeds mix with the harvest. In the USA, 10 plants per square meter cut the yield of drill seeded rice by 24 to 31 percent. So it makes sense to control it early, before it seeds.
